question: A tank endorsement is generally required for a Class A or B CDL vehicle hauling liquid in a tank when the tank(s) meet what capacity thresholds?
choice_a: An individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate rated capacity of 1000 gallons or more
choice_b: Any tank of any size used to haul any liquid
choice_c: An aggregate rated capacity of more than 5000 gallons only
choice_d: An individual rated capacity of more than 50 gallons regardless of aggregate capacity
explanation: The manual states a tank endorsement is required if the vehicle needs a Class A or B CDL and hauls a liquid or liquid gas in a tank or tanks having an individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate rated capacity of 1000 gallons or more.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8 Tank Vehicles (Introduction)

question: What are the consequences of driving a tank vehicle with a known leak?
choice_a: It is a crime; you will be cited, prevented from driving further, and may be liable for spill clean-up
choice_b: Only a warning is issued for a first offense
choice_c: None, as long as the spill is small
choice_d: You must simply report it at the next scheduled inspection
explanation: The manual states that carrying liquids or gases in a leaking tank is a crime; you will be cited and prevented from driving further, and you may also be liable for the clean-up of any spill.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.1.1 Leaks

question: Besides the tank's body or shell, what other components should you check for leaks on a tank vehicle?
choice_a: The intake, discharge, and cut-off valves; pipes, connections, and hoses (especially at joints); and manhole covers and vents
choice_b: Only the tires and wheels
choice_c: Only the fuel gauge
choice_d: Only the trailer hand valve
explanation: The manual lists checking the intake, discharge, and cut-off valves for correct position, pipes/connections/hoses for leaks especially around joints, and manhole covers and vents for gaskets and correct closure.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.1.1 Leaks

question: What does the manual say about driving a tank vehicle with open valves or manhole covers?
choice_a: It is acceptable for short distances at low speed
choice_b: Never drive a tank vehicle with open valves or manhole covers
choice_c: It is only a problem when hauling hazardous materials
choice_d: It is allowed if the vapor recovery kit is functioning
explanation: The manual explicitly instructs: never drive a tank vehicle with open valves or manhole covers.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.1.2 Check Special Purpose Equipment

question: Which of the following is listed as special purpose equipment that must be checked and confirmed working on some tank vehicles?
choice_a: Vapor recovery kits, grounding and bonding cables, emergency shut-off systems, and a built-in fire extinguisher
choice_b: A second steering wheel
choice_c: A rear-facing radar unit
choice_d: A supplemental alcohol evaporator
explanation: The manual lists vapor recovery kits, grounding and bonding cables, emergency shut-off systems, and a built-in fire extinguisher as special purpose equipment to check.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.1.2 Check Special Purpose Equipment

question: Why are liquid tankers especially easy to roll over?
choice_a: They lack any form of suspension
choice_b: They have narrower tires than other trucks
choice_c: Their high center of gravity makes them top-heavy; tests show tankers can turn over at the speed limits posted for curves
choice_d: They are always overloaded beyond legal weight limits
explanation: The manual states high center of gravity makes the vehicle top-heavy and easy to roll over, and tests have shown that tankers can turn over at the speed limits posted for curves, so drivers should take curves well below posted speeds.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.2.1 High Center of Gravity

question: What is liquid surge, and what effect can it have when coming to a stop?
choice_a: The buildup of static electricity inside the tank
choice_b: A pressure spike that automatically triggers the emergency brakes
choice_c: A chemical reaction between different cargo types
choice_d: Movement of liquid in a partially filled tank; when the wave hits the end of the tank, it tends to push the truck in the direction the wave is moving
explanation: The manual explains that liquid surge results from movement of the liquid in partially filled tanks, and when the wave hits the end of the tank, it tends to push the truck in the direction the wave is moving.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.2.2 Danger of Surge

question: What additional danger does liquid surge create if the truck is on a slippery surface such as ice?
choice_a: It only affects tank pressure readings
choice_b: The wave can shove a stopped truck out into an intersection
choice_c: It has no additional effect on ice
choice_d: It causes the tank to freeze solid
explanation: The manual warns that if the truck is on a slippery surface such as ice, the surge wave can shove a stopped truck out into an intersection.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.2.2 Danger of Surge

question: What must a driver pay attention to when loading and unloading a liquid tank divided into smaller tanks by bulkheads?
choice_a: The color of each liquid being loaded
choice_b: Bulkheads eliminate the need to consider weight distribution
choice_c: Weight distribution, so as not to put too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle
choice_d: Only the total volume, regardless of position
explanation: The manual states that when loading and unloading the smaller tanks created by bulkheads, the driver must pay attention to weight distribution and not put too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.2.3 Bulkheads

question: What do baffled liquid tanks do, and what surge risk remains even with baffles?
choice_a: Baffles eliminate all forms of liquid surge entirely
choice_b: Baffles only prevent side-to-side surge, not forward-backward surge
choice_c: Baffles are required on all food-grade tankers
choice_d: Baffles help control forward-and-backward surge, but side-to-side surge can still occur and cause a rollover
explanation: The manual explains that baffled tanks have bulkheads with holes that let liquid flow through, helping control forward and backward surge, but side-to-side surge can still occur, which can cause a rollover.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.2.4 Baffled Tanks

question: Why do un-baffled ('smooth bore') tanks usually carry food products such as milk?
choice_a: Sanitation regulations forbid the use of baffles because of the difficulty in cleaning the inside of the tank
choice_b: Food products cannot legally be transported in baffled tanks under any circumstances
choice_c: Smooth bore tanks weigh less than baffled tanks
choice_d: Baffles are more expensive to install than smooth bore tanks
explanation: The manual explains that un-baffled tanks are usually used for food products like milk because sanitation regulations forbid the use of baffles due to the difficulty of cleaning the inside of the tank.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.2.5 Un-baffled Tanks

question: Why must drivers be extremely cautious when starting and stopping an un-baffled ('smooth bore') tank?
choice_a: The cargo is always classified as hazardous material
choice_b: Forward-and-back liquid surge is very strong since there is nothing inside to slow the flow of liquid
choice_c: The tank has no brakes
choice_d: Smooth bore tanks cannot use ABS
explanation: The manual explains that un-baffled tankers have nothing inside to slow down the flow of liquid, so forward-and-back surge is very strong, requiring extreme caution, especially when starting and stopping.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.2.5 Un-baffled Tanks

question: What is 'outage' when loading a cargo tank with liquid?
choice_a: The amount of liquid lost to leaks during transit
choice_b: The room left for liquid expansion, since liquids expand as they warm and you must never load a cargo tank totally full
choice_c: The distance the tank protrudes past the trailer frame
choice_d: A discount applied when a tank is underfilled
explanation: The manual defines outage as the room left for liquid expansion; you must never load a cargo tank totally full because liquids expand as they warm, and different liquids require different outage amounts.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.2.6 Outage

question: Why might a full tank of a dense liquid, such as some acids, need to be only partially filled?
choice_a: Acids corrode the tank walls if loaded fully
choice_b: Dense liquids are always classified as hazardous material requiring partial loads
choice_c: Partial filling is only a fuel-economy preference
choice_d: A full tank of dense liquid may exceed legal weight limits
explanation: The manual states a full tank of dense liquid, such as some acids, may exceed legal weight limits, so tanks may often only be partially filled with heavy liquids.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.2.7 How Much to Load?

question: According to the manual, what three factors determine how much liquid to load into a tank?
choice_a: Only the tank's total volume capacity
choice_b: The color of the liquid, the ambient temperature, and the driver's experience level
choice_c: The amount the liquid will expand in transit, the weight of the liquid, and legal weight limits
choice_d: The tank's paint color, the trailer's age, and the route distance
explanation: The manual lists the amount the liquid will expand in transit, the weight of the liquid, and legal weight limits as the factors that determine how much liquid to load into a tank.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.2.7 How Much to Load?

question: What braking technique helps control liquid surge while driving a tank vehicle?
choice_a: Brake only at the very last moment for maximum control
choice_b: Rely exclusively on the parking brake to slow down
choice_c: Keep a steady pressure on the brakes, don't release too soon when coming to a stop, and brake far in advance while increasing following distance
choice_d: Pump the brakes rapidly on approach to every stop
explanation: The manual advises keeping a steady pressure on the brakes, not releasing too soon when stopping, and braking far in advance of a stop while increasing following distance to control surge.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.3.2 Controlling Surge

question: What driving technique does the manual recommend for tank vehicles approaching a curve?
choice_a: Accelerate before the curve, then brake hard through it
choice_b: Maintain the posted speed limit exactly throughout the curve
choice_c: Slow down before the curve, then accelerate slightly through the curve, since the posted speed may be too fast for a tank vehicle
choice_d: Curves require no special technique for tank vehicles
explanation: The manual instructs slowing down before curves, then accelerating slightly through the curve, since the posted speed for a curve may be too fast for a tank vehicle.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.3.3 Curves

question: According to the manual, how does an empty tank vehicle's stopping distance compare to a full one, and how do wet roads affect stopping distance?
choice_a: Empty tank vehicles always stop faster, and wet roads have no effect
choice_b: Full and empty tank vehicles stop identically, and wet roads reduce stopping distance
choice_c: Stopping distance is unaffected by load or road condition in tank vehicles
choice_d: Empty tank vehicles may take longer to stop than full ones, and wet roads double the normal stopping distance
explanation: The manual states that wet roads double the normal stopping distance, and empty tank vehicles may take longer to stop than full ones.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.3.4 Stopping Distance

question: What can happen on a tank trailer if the drive wheels or trailer wheels begin to skid?
choice_a: The vehicle may jackknife
choice_b: The ABS system disengages permanently
choice_c: Nothing different happens compared to a dry van trailer
choice_d: The tank automatically depressurizes to prevent rollover
explanation: The manual warns that on tank trailers, if the drive wheels or trailer wheels begin to skid, the vehicle may jackknife, and when any vehicle starts to skid you must take action to restore traction to the wheels.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.3.5 Skids

question: Because of the high center of gravity and liquid surge, how should a tank vehicle driver start, slow down, and stop?
choice_a: Very smoothly, and also make smooth turns and lane changes
choice_b: Speed and braking technique are not affected by cargo type
choice_c: Only in a straight line, never turning while decelerating
choice_d: As abruptly as possible to minimize time spent braking
explanation: The manual states that because of the high center of gravity and the surge of the liquid, drivers must start, slow down, and stop very smoothly, and make smooth turns and lane changes.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.3.1 Drive Smoothly

question: If a tank vehicle driver must make a quick stop to avoid a crash, what braking methods does the manual recommend, and what related risk should the driver keep in mind?
choice_a: Use only the trailer hand valve for emergency stops
choice_b: Slam on the brakes and turn the steering wheel sharply at the same time
choice_c: Use controlled or stab braking, and remember that steering quickly while braking may roll the vehicle over
choice_d: Downshift multiple gears simultaneously while braking hard
explanation: The manual advises using controlled or stab braking for a quick stop to avoid a crash, and reminds drivers that if you steer quickly while braking, your vehicle may roll over.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, 8.3.2 Controlling Surge
